title: Power Law of Logarithms
overview: How long until an investment doubles? When the unknown is an **exponent**, the **power law of logarithms**, $\log_b x^n = n\log_b x$, brings it down where you can solve for it. The same idea gives the **change of base formula**, which lets you evaluate and graph logarithms with any base using the LOG key on your calculator.
objectives: State, prove and apply the power law of logarithms.
Evaluate logarithms involving powers and radicals.
Solve equations of the form $b^x = m$ using common logarithms.
Evaluate and graph logarithms with any base using the change of base formula.
Solve compound interest, depreciation and other real-world problems with unknown exponents.
Recognise incorrect uses of the power law.

lessons.title: The problem: an unknown in the exponent
lessons.body:
Suppose you invest 100 dollars at 5% interest, compounded annually. After $t$ years you have

$$A = 100(1.05)^t$$

When will the money double? Set $A = 200$:

$$200 = 100(1.05)^t \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2 = 1.05^t$$

You could guess and check (or read a graph), but you can't "undo" the exponent with ordinary algebra. In logarithmic form the answer is $t = \log_{1.05} 2$ — but most calculators only have **LOG** (base 10). We need two new tools: the **power law** and the **change of base formula**.

lessons.title: The power law of logarithms
lessons.body:
Look at the pattern:

| $\log 2$ | $\log 4 = \log 2^2$ | $\log 8 = \log 2^3$ | $\log 16 = \log 2^4$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.301 | 0.602 | 0.903 | 1.204 |

Each value is a multiple of $\log 2$: $\log 2^n = n\log 2$. In general:

$$\boxed{\log_b x^n = n\log_b x}\qquad b > 0,\ b \neq 1,\ x > 0,\ n \in \mathbb{R}$$

**Why it works (proof).** Let $w = \log_b x$, so $x = b^w$. Raise both sides to the power $n$: $x^n = (b^w)^n = b^{wn}$. In logarithmic form, $\log_b x^n = wn = n\log_b x$.

> **In words:** the exponent of the argument can be brought down in front of the logarithm. That is exactly the step that "frees" an unknown exponent.

**Using it to evaluate:**

* $\log_3 9^4 = 4\log_3 9 = 4(2) = 8$
* $\log_2 8^5 = 5\log_2 8 = 5(3) = 15$
* $\log 0.001^2 = 2\log 10^{-3} = 2(-3) = -6$
* $\log_5 \sqrt{125} = \log_5 125^{1/2} = \frac12(3) = \frac32$ — write radicals as fractional exponents first.

lessons.title: Solving for an unknown exponent
lessons.body:
**Strategy:** isolate the power, take the common logarithm of both sides, apply the power law, then divide.

$$2 = 1.05^t$$
$$\log 2 = \log 1.05^t$$
$$\log 2 = t\log 1.05$$
$$t = \frac{\log 2}{\log 1.05} \approx 14.2$$

The investment doubles in about **14.2 years**.

Note that the starting amount cancelled out: doubling time depends only on the growth rate, not on how much you invest. (The "rule of 72" estimate: $72 \div 5 \approx 14.4$ years.)

**Careful:** $\frac{\log 2}{\log 1.05}$ is a *quotient* of logs. It is **not** $\log\frac{2}{1.05}$ and not $\log 2 - \log 1.05$.

lessons.title: The change of base formula
lessons.body:
The same technique evaluates a logarithm with **any** base. Let $x = \log_b m$. Then $b^x = m$, so $\log b^x = \log m$, giving $x\log b = \log m$:

$$\boxed{\log_b m = \frac{\log m}{\log b}}\qquad m > 0,\ b > 0,\ b \neq 1$$

* $\log_5 17 = \frac{\log 17}{\log 5} \approx 1.760$ — sensible, since $5^1 = 5 < 17 < 25 = 5^2$.
* $\log_{1/2} 10 = \frac{\log 10}{\log 0.5} = \frac{1}{-0.301} \approx -3.322$.

**Graphing any base.** To graph $f(x) = \log_5 x$ on a calculator, enter $y = \frac{\log x}{\log 5}$. Or graph the inverse $y = 5^x$ and reflect it in $y = x$.

```plot
title: Graphing log base 5 with the change of base formula
f: log(x)/log(5) | label=y = log₅ x
f: 5^x | dashed; label=y = 5^x
f: x | dashed
domain: -3, 8
range: -3, 8
points: (1,0), (5,1)
```

lessons.title: What the power law does NOT say
lessons.body:
The power law applies only when the **argument** is raised to a power.

| Statement | True? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| $\log x^3 = 3\log x$ | ✓ | power law |
| $(\log x)^3 = 3\log x$ | ✗ | the *log* is cubed, not the argument; e.g. $x = 100$: $8 \neq 6$ |
| $\log(3x) = 3\log x$ | ✗ | e.g. $x = 10$: $\log 30 \approx 1.48 \neq 3$ |
| $\log_2 8^{1/3} = \frac13\log_2 8 = 1$ | ✓ | fractional exponents are allowed |

Also remember the restrictions: $x > 0$. For example $\log x^2$ is defined for all $x \neq 0$, but $2\log x$ only for $x > 0$, so the two graphs are not identical.

keyTerms.definition: $\log_b m = \frac{\log m}{\log b}$; expresses a logarithm in any base using common logarithms.
The time for an exponentially growing quantity to double; for $A = P(1 + i)^t$ it is $t = \frac{\log 2}{\log(1 + i)}$.
Interest added to the principal each period, giving $A = P(1 + i)^n$ where $i$ is the rate per period.

formulas.name: Solving b^x = m
formulas.meaning: Take common logs of both sides and apply the power law.

formulas.name: Compound interest
formulas.meaning: $P$ principal, $i$ interest rate per compounding period, $n$ number of periods.

workedExamples.title: Doubling time
workedExamples.problem: How long does an investment at 5% compounded annually take to double?

workedExamples.title: Thickness of sunglasses
workedExamples.problem: Light through sunglasses glass $x$ mm thick has intensity $I = I_0(0.8)^x$. How thick must the glass be to block 25% of the light?

misconceptions.fact: The power law only applies to a power **of the argument**: $\log x^2 = 2\log x$. For $x = 1000$: $(\log 1000)^2 = 9$ but $2\log 1000 = 6$.
The 5 is a factor, not an exponent. $\log(5x) \neq 5\log x$.
A quotient of logarithms is not the log of a quotient. Evaluate the numerator and denominator separately.

misconceptions.myth: The doubling time depends on how much you invest.
misconceptions.fact: In $2P = P(1 + i)^t$ the principal cancels; doubling time depends only on the rate.
Change of base gives $\frac{\log m}{\log b}$, a quotient of two logs.

realWorld.title: Rule of 72
realWorld.body: Bankers estimate doubling time by dividing 72 by the annual percentage rate. The power law shows where it comes from: $t = \frac{\log 2}{\log(1 + i)}$ is close to $\frac{72}{100i}$ for small rates.

realWorld.title: Spacecraft docking
realWorld.body: Braking thrusters reduce the distance to a space station exponentially, so the time to reach docking range is a logarithm, e.g. $t = \log_{0.5}\left(\frac{d}{1000}\right)$.

realWorld.title: Car depreciation
realWorld.body: A vehicle losing 25% per year is worth $V = V_0(0.75)^t$; logs tell you when it is worth half the purchase price.

realWorld.title: Atmospheric pressure
realWorld.body: Air pressure drops exponentially with altitude ($P = 101.3(1.133)^{-d}$), so climbers and pilots use logarithms to work out altitude from a pressure reading.

practice.question: Solve $2 = 1.08^t$.
practice.hint: This is a doubling time at 8%.

practice.question: A 500-dollar investment earns 7% compounded annually. How long until it triples?

summary: Power law: $\log_b x^n = n\log_b x$ — an exponent on the argument can be moved to the front.
To solve $b^x = m$, take common logs: $x = \frac{\log m}{\log b}$.
Change of base: $\log_b m = \frac{\log m}{\log b}$ lets you evaluate or graph a logarithm with any base.
Doubling and tripling times of investments depend only on the interest rate.
The power law does not apply to $(\log x)^n$ or $\log(nx)$.

questions.text: An investment earns {{rp}}% interest, compounded annually. Its value after $t$ years is $A(t) = {{p}}({{g}})^t$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the initial value and find the value after 4 years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How long will it take the investment to double?

parts.label: c
parts.text: How long will it take to triple?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why your answers do not depend on the initial principal.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $A(0) = {{p}}$ dollars (the coefficient, since ${{g}}^0 = 1$). $A(4) = {{p}}({{g}})^4 \approx {{p*(1+rp/100)^4:5}}$ dollars.

(b) Double: $2 = ({{g}})^t \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{\log 2}{\log {{g}}} \approx {{log(2)/log(1+rp/100):3}}$ years.

(c) Triple: $t = \dfrac{\log 3}{\log {{g}}} \approx {{log(3)/log(1+rp/100):3}}$ years.

(d) Neither answer depends on {{p}}: dividing both sides by the principal leaves $({{g}})^t = 2$ or $3$. The doubling time depends only on the rate. (Rule of 72 check: $72 \div {{rp}} \approx {{72/rp:3}}$ years.)

rubric.point: Correct initial value and value after 4 years
Sets up and solves the doubling equation with logs

questions.text: Evaluate each logarithm, correct to three decimal places, using the change of base formula. Then check that each answer is reasonable.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $\log_{ {{b}} } {{m}} = \dfrac{\log {{m}}}{\log {{b}}} \approx {{log(m)/log(b):4}}$. Reasonable: ${{b}}^{ {{floor(log(m)/log(b))}} } = {{b^floor(log(m)/log(b))}} < {{m}} < {{b^(floor(log(m)/log(b))+1)}}$.

(b) $\log_{0.5} {{n}} = \dfrac{\log {{n}}}{\log 0.5} \approx {{log(n)/log(0.5):4}}$. Negative, as expected: $0.5$ must be raised to a negative power to give a number greater than 1.

(c) $\log_{ {{b}} } 0.{{z}} = \dfrac{\log 0.{{z}}}{\log {{b}}} \approx {{log(z/10)/log(b):4}}$ (negative because the argument is between 0 and 1).

questions.text: Prove the power law of logarithms, $\log_b x^n = n\log_b x$, and use it to explain why the change of base formula works.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Power law.** Let $w = \log_b x$. In exponential form $x = b^w$. Raise both sides to the power $n$: $x^n = (b^w)^n = b^{wn}$ (power law of exponents). Rewrite in logarithmic form: $\log_b x^n = wn$. Substitute $w = \log_b x$: $\log_b x^n = n\log_b x$. ∎

**Change of base.** Let $y = \log_b m$, so $b^y = m$. Take the common logarithm of both sides: $\log b^y = \log m$. By the power law, $y\log b = \log m$, so $y = \frac{\log m}{\log b}$. Therefore $\log_b m = \frac{\log m}{\log b}$ (valid for $m > 0$, $b > 0$, $b \neq 1$, since $\log b \neq 0$).

rubric.point: Introduces w = log_b x and rewrites in exponential form
Raises to the power n using exponent laws
Converts back and substitutes to complete the proof
Derives change of base using the power law

questions.text: A student writes: "$\log(mx) = m\log x$ and $\log(x^n) = (\log x)^n$." Evaluate both claims.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $\log(mx) = m\log x$ is **false** in general. Counter-example: $m = 3$, $x = 10$: $\log 30 \approx 1.477$ but $3\log 10 = 3$. Graphically, $y = \log(3x)$ is a horizontal compression of $\log x$ (a vertical shift of about 0.477), while $y = 3\log x$ is a vertical stretch — different graphs. (They agree only at special points.)

(b) $\log(x^n) = (\log x)^n$ is **false** in general. Counter-example: $x = 1000$, $n = 2$: $\log 10^6 = 6$ but $(\log 1000)^2 = 9$. The correct statement is the power law $\log(x^n) = n\log x$; $(\log x)^n$ raises the *log* to a power.

(c) The power law applies only when the argument itself is raised to a power.

rubric.point: Shows the first claim is false with a numerical counter-example
Shows the second claim is false with a counter-example
States the correct power law and when it applies

questions.text: A spacecraft is approaching a space station. When it is 1000 km away, reverse thrusters fire. The time, $t$, in hours, to reach a distance $d$ kilometres from the station is $t = \log_{0.5}\left(\dfrac{d}{1000}\right)$. Docking can begin once the craft is within {{dk}} km.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How long after the thrusters first fire should docking procedures begin?

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the domain and range of the function and explain what they represent.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $t = \log_{0.5}\left(\dfrac{ {{dk}} }{1000}\right) = \dfrac{\log {{dk/1000}}}{\log 0.5} \approx {{log(dk/1000)/log(0.5):3}}$ h after the thrusters fire.

(b) Domain: $0 < d \le 1000$ (the craft starts 1000 km away and the distance stays positive). Range: $t \ge 0$. As $d \to 0$, $t \to \infty$ — the model says the craft halves its distance every hour, so in theory it never quite arrives. The model only applies during braking.

questions.text: An investment pays {{rp}}% interest per year, compounded quarterly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the amount, $A$, as a function of time, $t$, in years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How long will it take to double?

parts.label: c
parts.text: How long will it take to triple?

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Quarterly rate $i = \frac{ {{rp}} }{400} = {{rp/400}}$; after $t$ years there are $4t$ periods: $A = P\left(1 + {{rp/400}}\right)^{4t}$.

(b) Double: $2 = ({{1 + rp/400}})^{4t} \Rightarrow 4t = \dfrac{\log 2}{\log {{1 + rp/400}}} \Rightarrow t \approx {{log(2)/(4*log(1+rp/400)):3}}$ years.

(c) Triple: $t = \dfrac{\log 3}{4\log {{1 + rp/400}}} \approx {{log(3)/(4*log(1+rp/400)):3}}$ years.

rubric.point: Correct equation with quarterly rate and 4t periods

questions.text: Solve for $x$, correct to three decimal places.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) ${{k}} = \log({{c}}x) \Rightarrow {{c}}x = 10^{ {{k}} } \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{ {{10^k}} }{ {{c}} } \approx {{10^k/c:5}}$.

(b) ${{j}} = \log_3 x \Rightarrow x = 3^{ {{j}} } = {{3^j}}$.

(c) $x = \log_{ {{b}} } {{m}} = \dfrac{\log {{m}}}{\log {{b}}} \approx {{log(m)/log(b):4}}$.

(d) $12 = 2\log_5 x \Rightarrow \log_5 x = 6 \Rightarrow x = 5^6 = 15\,625$.

questions.text: The intensity, $I$, of light passing through sunglasses glass $x$ millimetres thick is $I(x) = I_0(0.8)^x$, where $I_0$ is the intensity entering the glass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How thick should the glass be to block {{blk}}% of the light?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Does doubling this thickness block twice as much light? Explain.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Blocking {{blk}}% means {{100-blk}}% is transmitted: ${{(100-blk)/100}} = 0.8^x$.

$x = \dfrac{\log {{(100-blk)/100}}}{\log 0.8} \approx {{log((100-blk)/100)/log(0.8):3}}$ mm.

(b) Twice the thickness transmits $0.8^{2x} = ({{(100-blk)/100}})^2 = {{((100-blk)/100)^2:3}}$ of the light, so it blocks ${{100 - 100*((100-blk)/100)^2:3}}\%$ — not twice as much. Each millimetre removes the same *percentage* of the light remaining, not the same amount.

rubric.point: Sets up the equation using the transmitted fraction
Correct analysis of doubling the thickness

questions.text: A vehicle depreciates by {{d}}% each year. Its value, in dollars, after $t$ years is $V(t) = {{v0}}({{1 - d/100}})^t$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What was the initial value of the vehicle? How do you know?

parts.label: b
parts.text: How long until the vehicle is worth half its initial value?

parts.label: c
parts.text: After how many years is it worth {{v1}} dollars?

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The initial value is $V(0) = {{v0}}$ dollars, because any base to the power 0 is 1.

(b) Half value: $0.5 = ({{1 - d/100}})^t \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{\log 0.5}{\log {{1 - d/100}}} \approx {{log(0.5)/log(1-d/100):3}}$ years.

(c) Value below {{v1}} dollars: $({{1 - d/100}})^t = \frac{ {{v1}} }{ {{v0}} } \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{\log({{v1}}/{{v0}})}{\log {{1 - d/100}}} \approx {{log(v1/v0)/log(1-d/100):3}}$ years.

rubric.point: Correct time to fall to the given value

questions.text: Atmospheric pressure, $P$, in kilopascals, at an altitude of $d$ kilometres is modelled by $P = 101.3(1.133)^{-d}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the pressure at an altitude of {{h}} km.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How high is a climber who measures a pressure of {{p}} kPa?

parts.label: c
parts.text: By what percent does the pressure decrease for each kilometre of altitude? Explain.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $P({{h}}) = 101.3(1.133)^{-{{h}}} \approx {{101.3*1.133^(-h):3}}$ kPa.

(b) ${{p}} = 101.3(1.133)^{-d} \Rightarrow \dfrac{ {{p}} }{101.3} = 1.133^{-d}$

$\log\left(\dfrac{ {{p}} }{101.3}\right) = -d\log 1.133 \Rightarrow d = -\dfrac{\log({{p}}/101.3)}{\log 1.133} \approx {{-log(p/101.3)/log(1.133):3}}$ km.

(c) The pressure is multiplied by $1.133^{-1} \approx 0.883$ for every kilometre climbed, so it falls by about 11.7% of its current value each kilometre — exponential decay.

rubric.point: Correct pressure at the given altitude
Isolates the power and takes logs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate without using the power law.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate using the power law.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which method do you prefer? Why?

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Without the power law: $16^{ {{n}} } = (2^4)^{ {{n}} } = 2^{ {{4*n}} }$, so $\log_2 16^{ {{n}} } = {{4*n}}$.

(b) With the power law: $\log_2 16^{ {{n}} } = {{n}}\log_2 16 = {{n}}(4) = {{4*n}}$.

(c) Both give {{4*n}}. The power law avoids working with very large numbers (here $16^{ {{n}} } = {{16^n}}$), so it is usually quicker and less error-prone.

questions.text: According to the power law, $\log x^2 = 2\log x$. Consider the functions $f(x) = \log x^2$ and $g(x) = 2\log x$.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $f(x) = \log x^2$ is defined whenever $x^2 > 0$, i.e. for all $x \neq 0$. $g(x) = 2\log x$ is defined only for $x > 0$.

(b) For $x > 0$ the two functions are identical (the power law holds). For $x < 0$, $g$ is undefined but $f$ is defined: $f(-10) = \log 100 = 2$. The graph of $f$ has two branches symmetric about the $y$-axis (it is an even function); $g$ has only the right branch.

(c) The power law $\log_b x^n = n\log_b x$ requires $x > 0$. Using it on $\log x^2$ for negative $x$ would lose part of the graph, so the restriction matters.

rubric.point: Explains the graphs agree for x > 0 and differ for x < 0
Links to the restriction x > 0 in the power law

questions.text: Describe two different methods for graphing $f(x) = \log_{ {{b}} } x$ and explain why each works.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Method 1 — inverse.** Graph $y = {{b}}^x$ (points $(-1, \tfrac{1}{ {{b}} })$, $(0, 1)$, $(1, {{b}})$), then reflect it in the line $y = x$ to get $(\tfrac{1}{ {{b}} }, -1)$, $(1, 0)$, $({{b}}, 1)$. It works because $\log_{ {{b}} } x$ is the inverse of ${{b}}^x$.

**Method 2 — change of base.** Enter $y = \dfrac{\log x}{\log {{b}}}$ into a graphing calculator. It works because $\log_{ {{b}} } x = \frac{\log x}{\log {{b}}}$ for all $x > 0$; this is just $y = \log x$ stretched vertically by the factor $\frac{1}{\log {{b}}} \approx {{1/log(b):3}}$.

Key features either way: domain $x > 0$, $x$-intercept 1, asymptote $x = 0$, passes through $({{b}}, 1)$.

rubric.point: Describes the inverse/reflection method with points

questions.text: The population of a city is {{p0}} and is increasing by {{r}}% per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the population as a function of time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How long will it take the population to double?

parts.label: c
parts.text: After how many years will the population reach 100 000?

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $P(t) = {{p0}}({{g}})^t$ where $t$ is in years. (Growth factor $1 + \frac{ {{r}} }{100}$.)

(b) Double: $2 = {{g}}^t \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{\log 2}{\log {{g}}} \approx {{log(2)/log(1+r/100):3}}$ years.

(c) ${{target}} = {{p0}}({{g}})^t \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{\log({{target}}/{{p0}})}{\log {{g}}} \approx {{log(target/p0)/log(1+r/100):3}}$ years.

rubric.point: Correct time to reach the target
